question:
A 67-year-old man with a decade-long history of COPD presents with worsening chronic cough
producing sputum and increasing shortness of breath. He denies any changes in the appearance of his
phlegm. Currently, he is unable to climb a single flight of stairs without experiencing severe dyspnea.
His beta natriuretic peptide (BNP) level is normal, and a transthoracic echocardiogram from three
months ago shows no change, with an ejection fraction of 30%. Which of the following is the most
appropriate treatment? Answer Choices: (A) Start azithromycin and observe for 72 hours (B) Start
furosemide and monitor daily weights (C) Start inhaled corticosteroids (D) Add tiotropium to current
regimen (E) Add oral prednisone for 5 days (F) Add a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) (G) Initiate
pulmonary rehabilitation program (H) Initiate non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (I) Increase
dose of Ipratropium and albuterol and observe for 72 hours (J) Start levofloxacin and observe for 72
hours
 A. Initiate non-invasive positive pressure ventilation
B. Start furosemide and monitor daily weights
C. Start azithromycin and observe for 72 hours
D. Add a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA)
E. Start inhaled corticosteroids
F. Start levofloxacin and observe for 72 hours
G. Initiate pulmonary rehabilitation program
H. Increase dose of Ipratropium and albuterol and observe for 72 hours
I. Add oral prednisone for 5 days
J. Add tiotropium to current regimen
